stimulus.text:
“I long to hear that you have declared an independency — and by the way in the new Code of Laws which I suppose it will be necessary for you to make I desire you would Remember the Ladies, and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the Husbands. Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could. If perticuliar care and attention is not paid to the Laidies we are determined to foment a Rebelion, and will not hold ourselves bound by any Laws in which we have no voice, or Representation.”
— Abigail Adams to John Adams, Braintree, March 31, 1776 (abridged; spelling as in the original)
stimulus.source_note: Abigail Adams to John Adams, March 31, 1776. Public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, B. Evolving Ideas on Gender

stem: Which of the following best describes how the idea of “republican motherhood” answered the hope in Adams's letter?

options.text: It gave married women the vote in the new state constitutions
options.misconception: No state gave women the vote in its constitution; republican motherhood was about education and raising sons, not voting.

options.text: It ended the legal rule that a wife's identity belonged to her husband
options.misconception: That rule, coverture, stayed in place; republican motherhood left married women's legal standing unchanged.

options.text: It let women serve as voters and officeholders in the new republic
options.misconception: Women held no offices and did not vote under the new governments; the idea kept them out of formal politics.

options.text: It gave women a role raising republican sons, while keeping them out of politics

rationales.D: Background from the books: republican motherhood said women mattered to the republic because they raised virtuous sons — and that meant women needed schooling. It widened women's education while leaving their legal and political standing where it was.
rationales.A: The vote is not part of republican motherhood; the idea gave women a teaching role at home, not a ballot.
rationales.B: Coverture was not ended by this idea; a wife's legal identity still belonged to her husband.
rationales.C: Officeholding and voting stayed closed to women; the new role was domestic, not political.
rationales.general:
1. Name Adams's hope. A new legal order that treats wives less like subjects.
2. Background: republican motherhood offered schooling for women so they could raise republican sons.
3. Background: it offered no vote, no office, and no change to a wife's legal standing.
Remember: a bigger role is not the same as equal standing — ask what changed and what stayed put.
